newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico lengthens it domestic debt profile.
newsitem.headline: Mexico lengthens it domestic debt profile.

text.p: Mexico is steadily lengthening the maturity of its domestic debt by offering a larger number of its longer-term development bonds, or Bondes.
At the same time, the Mexican government is considering offering longer-term Cetes, or treasury bills, officials said.
While the Banco de Mexico has been holding the amount of Cetes that it auctions each week at 3.3 billion, it has stepped up the amount of Bondes sold at its weekly primary auctions.
The central bank issues both one and two-year Bondes, which up-to-now have been mainly bought primarily within Mexico. The longest term Cetes issued now are for one year.
Analysts expect the market for longer-term peso-denominated Mexican paper to grow rapidly this year, once a number of new private pension funds start offering their services.
The government recently gave final approval to 12 companies to operate the new private pension funds known as Afores.

"I think that it is normal for Mexico to look now into making longer issues in the domestic market and as the pension fund reform goes forward the need for these kind of instruments is going to prevail," Finance Ministry spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela told Reuters.
"Cetes are short-term oriented debt and the market is getting deeper, so you have to take advantage of this and try to issue longer-term transactions," Valenzuela said.

The number of outstanding Bondes, government development bonds that pay a variable premium over the one-month Cetes rate, has risen steadily, and their total market value now stands higher than Cetes.
Mexico had offered two-year Cetes, but stopped issuing them after the sharp 1994 peso devaluation, which disrupted the economy.
But now the government is looking at extending Cetes maturities.
"You have to look at the advantages and disadvantages of each of the instruments that we have and also why not also think about longer-term Cetes," Valenzuela said.
"That gives the possibility of avoiding roll-over transaction costs, which are normally higher in the Cetes," he added.
The number of outstanding Bondes started 1996 at about 36 billion pesos, compared with outstanding Cetes with a market value of 44.0 billion pesos.
As of January 30 this year, the total market value of Cetes was 59.53 billion pesos - with 18.21 billion pesos held offshore, 39.60 billion pesos by residents and 1.72 billion pesos by banks.
The market value of the Bondes, however, was 62.84 billion pesos as of January 30, with only 1.21 billion pesos worth being held offshore.
Some debt analysts and Mexican banks have recently been recommending Bondes for peso-based investors, saying the floating rate paper is a good alternative to Cetes.
They say the downside in rates is minimal now and if rates rise the floating rate Bondes will pick up the increase.

"The Bondes market will keep growing. Although there is uncertainty over where rates will go in the future, they pay a premium that is relatively certain," said one Mexico City economist who declined to be identified.
However, some foreign investors prefer to stick with Cetes.

"I can buy them (Bondes), but I just feel that the liquidity in Cetes is better and returns are equal or close to it, so it doesn't make a heck of a lot of sense," said one U.S.-based portfolio manager.
There are also smaller amounts of other money-market instruments in the Mexican market.
